newsitem.title: UK: As equities star, non-oil commodities are dull.
newsitem.headline: As equities star, non-oil commodities are dull.

text.p: Wall Street's run up to 6,000 failed to cheer commodity markets from where booming equities and bonds have siphoned speculative money, with the exception of crude oil which powered on with a rally to top $24 per barrel. Industrial metals were not helped when scrap dealer Herbert Black of Canada whose selling of the market earlier this year helped topple Japan's trading idol, Yasuo Hamanaka, took a "bearish" view of the copper price. He predicted at an industry convention that London Metal Exchange (LME) three-months copper might slip to $1,400 per tonne in 1998 under a weight of new production and of metal previously hoarded by Japan's Sumitomo Corp and others. Hamanaka had held big stocks of copper before his June 14 dismissal by Sumitomo Corp and its accusations that he ran up losses of $2.6 billion on maverick trades.
Black was among dealers who sensed that his long position was vulnerable and who sold against him.
Copper ended London's afternoon just above $1,900 per tonne and easier from Friday on a day when sluggish range trading characterized most commodities except oil.
Aluminium dropped to its lowest in nearly 2-1/2 years at $1,332 a tonne, the weakest since May 1994. Brokers cited high stocks and a weak technical chart outlook.
But world benchmark November futures for North Sea crude oil broke back above $24 and stood 30 cents up on the day at $24.15 per barrel before easing slightly.
A scramble to recharge depleted winter heating oil stocks in Europe and the United States kept prices on the boil.

Worried refinery buyers, concerned that an early US cold snap could erode depleted stocks, hedged against price rises on futures exchanges and speculators bet on further gains. Gold stabilised after a fall below $380 per ounce early last week and traded little changed to close in London at $380.15. It edged up later.
